spots.name: Bettys
spots.label: Bettys Tea Rooms

text.access_note: St Helen's Square is open public space, but Bettys is a business, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
text.description:
Bettys is the tea room on the corner of St Helen's Square in the middle of York, and the square is where most visitors photograph it from. The corner window and the front of the building make a tidy subject, and the open space in front gives you room to step back and fit it all in. From some angles Mansion House appears behind, which helps show that this is a proper city-centre square rather than just a shopfront.

The usual picture is taken from across the square, looking towards the corner frontage. Stand far enough back that the whole corner sits in the frame with a little square in front of it. People tend to walk through the foreground, so take a few shots and pick the one with the cleanest gap. Queues can form along the front and around the side of the building at busy times, and they can block the view. If so, wait a minute or try a slightly different spot along the square.

It also works well after dark, when the corner window can be a feature of the picture. A 360-degree evening panorama has been taken here to capture it. Keep your phone upright for the facade, or turn it sideways if you want more of the square and the buildings around it. Please keep the doorway clear for people queuing.
text.directions_text: No Underground, rail or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for St Helen's Square in the centre of York. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of York, on St Helen's Square, with Mansion House visible from some angles across the square.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the corner of the building on one of the vertical lines so it looks straight. Leave a band of open square at the bottom of the frame. Keep the phone level, because tilting it makes the building lean. If the queue is in the way, wait for a gap or take a closer shot of the window with telephoto instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St Helen's Square (across the square from the Bettys corner frontage). The Bettys corner window and facade on St Helen's Square, with the square in front and Mansion House visible in the background from some angles.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the window or sky looks too bright. In the evening, let night mode work and hold the phone steady against your body. For a wider view of the square, try panorama mode and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Queues can build up at busy times and may block the view, so be ready to wait for a gap. In the evening the lit window can look good, so try a night-mode shot or a panorama then.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the corner window and facade. If you cannot step back far enough, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to include more of the square. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a closer view of the window.

spots.name: The Shambles
spots.label: The Shambles

text.access_note: The Shambles is an open public street that can be visited at any time, though the cobbles are uneven; check the official site before you go for anything about the shops along it.
text.description: The Shambles is a narrow lane in the middle of York, and it is probably the most photographed street in the city. Timber-framed houses lean towards each other, their upper floors jutting out over the cobbles by several feet, so the sky shrinks to a thin strip. That gives a phone photo strong lines and a lot of depth. Many of the buildings date from roughly 1350 to 1475, which means the street keeps a large amount of original medieval building fabric. The name comes from an Old English word for a butcher's bench or stall. In 1885 there were thirty-one butchers' shops here, and the last closed in the early twentieth century. Look for the meat hooks still hanging outside some shopfronts, with shelves below them. They make good close-up details. The tall, close buildings shade the street, so the light is soft and even rather than harsh. The street is at its busiest from mid-morning to late afternoon in summer, so for a clear view of the lane, go before 9am or after dark. Stand at the phone icon on the map and look south down the lane, so the leaning buildings close in on both sides and lead the eye away from you. The cobbles are uneven, so watch your footing while you hold up your phone.
text.directions_text: Start from the city centre around King's Square, Newgate or Pavement and walk to the middle of the street. The phone icon on the map is slightly north of where Little Shambles used to join the street. Walk to it and turn to face south. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.
text.geographic_location: The Shambles is in the historic centre of York, running between Newgate at the north end and Pavement at the south end. King's Square is nearby.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the lane in the centre, with the vertical lines of the buildings straight against the grid so they don't tilt. Hold the phone at chest height and keep it level, which also stops the buildings leaning backwards. If hanging signs and awnings cross the frame, shift a step to one side until you find a cleaner line. For a wider view of the whole crooked row of buildings, try King's Square, from a distance rather than inside the lane.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the photo shows the narrow lane running away from you, with the overhanging timber-framed upper storeys closing in on both sides.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the street itself to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright strip of sky doesn't turn white. Use night mode after dark, and hold your phone against a wall or your own chest to keep it steady. Live Photos can be handy for catching a moment when people have cleared from the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Before 9am, when the street is least crowded. Several guides also suggest after dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which shows the lane much as your eye sees it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the crowds or the narrow street stop you from stepping back, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, more compressed view of the leaning upper floors.

spots.alt: The Shambles, York: a narrow lane. Photo spot

text.access_note: Stonegate is a public street; check conditions locally before you go, and check the official site if you plan to go into any building.
text.description:
Stonegate is one of York's best-known streets for a photograph, and the reason is the view along it. Historic timber-fronted buildings line both sides, and at the far end York Minster rises above the rooftops. That gives you a ready-made picture with a foreground, a middle and a clear point of interest at the top.

The street is busy with visitors, so standing in the middle of it can mean people in every frame. A slightly calmer option is the edge of St Helen's Square, at the mouth of Stonegate. From there you look straight down the street towards the Minster, and you can take in the whole run of buildings without being jostled.

For a second angle, walk up towards the Minster and try Minster Yard. There the towers sit close above the buildings at the top of Stonegate, and the street leads down towards you.

Keep the phone level so the building fronts stay upright. Gridlines help with that. Wait a moment for a gap in the crowd, or accept a few figures as a sense of scale. An early or late visit usually means fewer people. Check your lens and screen are clean before you start, because it is easy to take a dozen shots in the same spot and find them all smeared.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the centre of York and look for St Helen's Square. Stonegate leads off the square to the north-east, towards the Minster. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.
text.geographic_location: Stonegate is in the centre of York, running from St Helen's Square towards York Minster.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the street so the buildings lead the eye towards the Minster, and use gridlines to keep the verticals straight. For a different angle, try Minster Yard at the top of the street, where the towers rise close above the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in St Helen's Square (from the square's edge at the mouth of Stonegate, looking down the street). A view straight down Stonegate with the Minster in the distance at the top of the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the Minster to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. Take a few frames in a row so you can pick the one with the fewest people.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day or later in the evening, when fewer people are likely to be in the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the full length of the street. Then try telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) to bring the Minster closer.
